claim: AMPA receptors are glutamate-gated ion channels whose four subunits assemble as a dimer-of-dimers.
source: Signal transduction at vertebrate excitatory synapses involves the rapid activation of AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionate) receptors, glutamate-gated ion channels whose four subunits assemble as a dimer-of-dimers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMPA receptor structure and is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy structures indicate that AMPA receptor dimers might undergo substantial lateral motions during gating, opening up the extracellular layer along the central twofold symmetry axis.
source: These structures indicate that dimers might undergo substantial lateral motions during gating, opening up the extracellular layer along the central twofold symmetry axis.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of cryo-EM structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: The extracellular layer of AMPA receptors can get trapped in stable, opened-up conformations, especially upon long exposures to glutamate.
source: Our data indicate that extracellular layer of AMPA receptors can get trapped in stable, opened-up conformations, especially upon long exposures to glutamate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the crosslinking experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stargazin limits the conformational flexibility of AMPA receptors.
source: In contrast, Stargazin limits this conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments comparing receptors with and without Stargazin.

claim: Under synaptic conditions with brief glutamate exposures and the presence of auxiliary proteins, extracellular domains of AMPA receptors likely stay compact during gating.
source: Thus, under synaptic conditions, where brief glutamate exposures and the presence of auxiliary proteins dominate, extracellular domains of AMPA receptors likely stay compact during gating.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents an inference about physiological conditions.

claim: AMPA receptors have fast kinetics that allow them to follow glutamate transients at rates above 100 Hz.
source: Their fast kinetics (Colquhoun et al., 1992; Geiger et al., 1995; Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000), as well as the physical attributes of synapses (Xu-Friedman and Regehr, 2003), allow them to follow glutamate transients at rates above 100 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: AMPA receptors are tetrameric ligand-gated ion channels consisting of three layers formed from distinct domains.
source: AMPA receptors are tetrameric ligand-gated ion channels. Ignoring their intracellular regions, they consist of three layers formed from distinct domains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about AMPA receptors, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The two extracellular layers of AMPA receptors assemble from amino-terminal domains (ATDs) and ligand-binding domains (LBDs).
source: The two extracellular layers assemble from amino-terminal domains and ligand-binding domains, ATDs and LBDs, respectively.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about AMPA receptor architecture.

claim: ATD dimers associate with high affinity (KD nM to μM).
source: Although the ATD dimers associate with high affinity (KD nM to μM (Zhao et al., 2017), the association of ATD dimers into a tetramer as well as of LBDs into dimers and tetramers is too weak to measure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: The association of ATD dimers into a tetramer and of LBDs into dimers and tetramers is too weak to measure.
source: Although the ATD dimers associate with high affinity (KD nM to μM (Zhao et al., 2017), the association of ATD dimers into a tetramer as well as of LBDs into dimers and tetramers is too weak to measure.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about AMPA receptor domain interactions.

claim: The LBD intra-dimer interface ruptures upon desensitization.
source: In case of the LBDs, this weak association has direct functional consequences, because the LBD intra-dimer interface ruptures upon desensitization (Sun et al., 2002; Armstrong et al., 2006; Dürr et al., 2014; Twomey et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: The synaptic cleft is scarcely wider than AMPA receptors are tall and has narrow edges.
source: The crowded and narrow synaptic cleft is scarcely wider than the receptors are tall themselves and has narrow edges (Zuber et al., 2005; Tao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies of synapses.

claim: Large conformational changes of AMPA receptor extracellular domains on the millisecond timescale could disrupt interactions with pre- and postsynaptic anchoring proteins.
source: For example, if the extracellular layer of AMPA receptors can undergo large conformational changes rapidly, that is on the millisecond timescale of fast excitatory transmission, this could disrupt possible interactions of the extracellular domains with the pre- and postsynaptic anchoring proteins (Elegheert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functional consequences, supported by a citation.

claim: Activity-dependent anchoring might be a way to regulate synaptic strength.
source: Activity-dependent anchoring might be a way to regulate synaptic strength (Constals et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Several agonist-bound structures suggest that local dimers in the ATD and LBD layer move apart from each other substantially.
source: Several agonist-bound structures (Nakagawa et al., 2005; Dürr et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2014) suggest that local dimers in the ATD and LBD layer move apart from each other substantially.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of multiple cited structural studies.

claim: Disulphide bonds and metal bridges can trap AMPA receptors in compact LBD arrangements.
source: Previously, we demonstrated disulphide bonds and metal bridges trapping receptors in compact, as opposed to 'open' LBD arrangements (Salazar et al., 2017; Baranovic et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Bifunctional methanethiosulfonate cross-linkers (bis-MTS) show specific combination with two free thiol groups provided by engineered cysteine residues.
source: These cross-linkers show specific combination with two free thiol groups, provided by cysteine residues that we engineered.
evidence: This is a known property of bis-MTS reagents and is demonstrated in the experiments.

claim: All bis-MTS cross-linkers (M1M to M10M) caused strong reduction of the peak current in V666C mutant when applied in the desensitized state.
source: As shown in Figure 2B and D, bis-MTS cross-linkers M1M to M10M all caused strong reduction of the peak current in V666C mutant when applied in the desensitized state.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: For V666C mutant, bis-MTS cross-linkers from 7 to 15 Å in length (M1M-M8M; 1 µM) inhibited ~90% of the peak current after a 1-min application.
source: For the V666C mutant, bis-MTS cross-linkers from 7 to 15 Å in length (M1M-M8M; 1 µM), inhibited ~90% of the peak current in the patch after a 1-min application (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the crosslinking experiments.

claim: The longest cross-linker (M10M) was the slowest to act on desensitized receptors, leading to less inhibition (~70%) in the first minute of exposure.
source: The longest (M10M) cross-linker was the slowest one to act (Figure 2F), leading to less inhibition (~70%) in the first minute of exposure.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: At 50 μM concentration, both M3M and M10M bis-MTS cross-linkers were roughly 50x faster to modify V666C receptors than at 1 μM.
source: Indeed, at 50 μM, both bis-MTS cross-linkers were roughly 50x faster to modify the receptors (τM3M = 0.2 s and τM10M = 1.7 s, Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bifunctional MTS reagents are capturing rapid transitions in receptor structure on the millisecond timescale.
source: These experiments indicate that bifunctional MTS reagents are capturing rapid transitions in receptor structure on the millisecond timescale.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the high-concentration crosslinking experiments.

claim: A665C sulfhydryl groups crosslink to each other during long exposures to 10 mM glutamate.
source: In case of A665C, the introduced cysteines linked to each other during long exposures to 10 mM glutamate, resulting in the peak current reduction of 0.62 ± 0.04 (n = 23, p < 10−7 vs. WT: 0.97 ± 0.03, n = 30), consistent with previous results (Lau et al., 2013; Yelshanskaya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with previous studies.

claim: Trapped A665C receptors recovered within seconds in reducing conditions (τ = 3.3 ± 0.4 s, n = 17).
source: In reducing conditions, the trapped A665C receptors recovered within seconds (grey dots in Figure 2C, τ = 3.3 ± 0.4 s, n = 17).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MTSEA failed to inhibit V666C or A665C receptors above glutamate-only control.
source: As shown in Figure 2D–E, MTSEA failed to inhibit either V666C or A665C above Glu-only control (V666C: 0.74 ± 0.008, n = 4, p = 0.1; A665C: 0.81 ± 0.06, n = 4, p = 0.06).
evidence: This is an experimental result demonstrating specificity of bifunctional crosslinking.

claim: Bifunctional MTS cross-linking was necessary for the peak current reduction observed in desensitizing AMPA receptors.
source: Thus, bifunctional MTS cross-linking was necessary for the peak current reduction observed in desensitizing AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of bifunctional and monofunctional MTS reagents.

claim: Limiting V666C separation of desensitized AMPA receptors to 18 Å causes inhibition, indicating further separation of the residues is possible.
source: These results demonstrate that limiting V666C separation of desensitized AMPA receptors to 18 Å causes inhibition, indicating further separation of the residues is possible, in good agreement with cryo-EM structures (Meyerson et al., 2014; Dürr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the crosslinking data and comparison with structural models.

claim: M3M cross-linker at 9 Å was the most effective in blocking desensitization of K493C receptors (Isteady-state/Ipeak = 80.8 ± 2%, n = 16).
source: At 9 Å, M3M was the most effective in blocking desensitization (Isteady-state/Ipeak = 80.8 ± 2%, n = 16, p < 10−7 vs. bis-MTS-free desensitization).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result from K493C crosslinking experiments.

claim: The bis-MTS length-dependent block of desensitization in K493C receptors strongly indicates the cross-linkers target introduced Cys mutations selectively.
source: The bis-MTS length-dependent block of desensitization in K493C receptors strongly indicates the cross-linkers target introduced Cys mutations selectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the K493C experiments demonstrating specificity.

claim: After trapping with M3M for 1 min, the peak current in V666C patches recovered very slowly, taking over 10 min (600 applications of Glu) to reach pre-trapping levels.
source: After the receptors were trapped with M3M for 1 min, the peak current in the patch did recover, but very slowly, taking over 10 min (600 applications of Glu) to reach the pre-trapping levels.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about recovery kinetics.

claim: With longer cross-linkers than M3M, the peak current was essentially irreversible over the timescales measured (20 min).
source: With longer cross-linkers, the peak current was essentially irreversible over the timescales we could measure (20 min; Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4.

claim: Multiple stable desensitized states trapped by bis-MTS are a possible explanation for the low-resolution cryo-EM structures of desensitized AMPA receptors in the absence of auxiliary subunits.
source: Multiple stable desensitized states trapped by bis-MTS are a possible explanation for the low-resolution cryo-EM structures of desensitized AMPA receptors in the absence of auxiliary subunits (Meyerson et al., 2014; Dürr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data in relation to structural studies.

claim: Block of desensitization with cyclothiazide reduced inhibition by bis-MTS cross-linkers in the first minute of exposure.
source: As shown in Figure 5, block of desensitization reduced inhibition by bis-MTS cross-linkers in the first minute of exposure (see Figure 5 – source data 1for statistics).
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing desensitizing and non-desensitizing conditions.

claim: With M3M, about 15% of active V666C receptors recovered from inhibition with a time constant of τ = 1.98 ± 0.2 s, n = 8.
source: For M3M, the recovery was still faster with τ = 1.98 ± 0.2 s, n = 8 (grey dots in Figure 5A), with about 15% the receptors recovering and leading to the final inhibition of 0.53 ± 0.03, n = 9.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result for active receptors.

claim: Active receptors displayed a distinct trapping profile from that of desensitized receptors, with a sharper profile indicative of less conformational heterogeneity.
source: With desensitization blocked, AMPA receptors displayed a distinct trapping profile from that of desensitized receptors (Figure 5C). All cross-linkers modulated active state less than the desensitized in the first minute of exposure, apart from M8M (15 Å; Figure 5B) and a fraction of active receptors trapped with the shorter cross-linkers (M1M and M3M) recovered fast from the trap. The trapping profile against linker length was sharper, indicative of less conformational heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing trapping profiles in Figure 5C.

claim: The preferred V666C sulfhydryl separation in the active state is around 15 Å, somewhat closer than 19 Å obtained in the cryo-EM structure of active GluA2.
source: At 12–15 Å (bMTSp, M6M and M8M), active receptors were trapped most effectively and without fast recovery; at 18 Å (M10M) the extent of trapping decreased (Figure 5—source data 1). This places the preferred V666C sulfhydryl separation in the active state around 15 Å, somewhat closer than 19 Å obtained in the cryo-EM structure of active GluA2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the active state trapping profile and comparison with structures.

claim: Non-desensitizing V666C receptors were not silently modified by M10M.
source: V666C receptors initially exposed to M10M in the presence of CTZ were modified to the same extent as naïve receptors (Ipeak post-trap/Ipeak pre-trap for V666C initially trapped in CTZ: 0.23 ± 0.04, n = 6 and for V666C never trapped in CTZ: 0.30 ± 0.03, n = 16, p = 0.07; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). Taken together, these results strongly suggest that non-desensitizing V666C receptors were not silently modified by M10M.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the CTZ unbinding experiment.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of AMPA receptors in complex with auxiliary subunits estimate reduced separation of V666C residues when compared to receptors without auxiliary proteins.
source: Recently, cryo-EM structures of AMPA receptors in complex with auxiliary subunits have been acquired in resting, active and desensitized states (Figure 1B) (Chen et al., 2017; Twomey et al., 2017a). These structures all estimate reduced separation of V666C residues when compared to receptors without auxiliary proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from published structural studies.

claim: The presence of auxiliary subunit Stargazin apparently protected V666C receptors from cross-linking by bis-MTS.
source: The trapping results summarized in Figure 6C show that the presence of auxiliary subunit Stg apparently protected V666C receptors from cross-linking by bis-MTS.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The KA/Glu ratio was not affected by bis-MTS trapping, indicating V666C-Stg complexes were being modified by bis-MTS cross-linkers.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, the KA/Glu ratio was not affected (before trap: 0.46 ± 0.03; after trap: 0.43 ± 0.02, n = 13; p = 0.2, paired randomization test), indicating V666C-Stg complexes were being modified by bis-MTS cross-linkers.
evidence: This is an experimental result demonstrating that complexes with Stargazin are modified.

claim: The trapping profile of V666C-Stg complexes is practically superposable onto the trapping profile of desensitized V666C receptors without Stg.
source: The trapping profile of V666C-Stg complexes (orange in Figure 6D) reflects the partial protection from trapping in the presence of Stg for all cross-linker lengths, but its overall shape is practically superposable onto the trapping profile of desensitized V666C receptors without Stg (red, dashed line in Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing trapping profiles in Figure 6D.

claim: The two trapping profile curves (with and without Stargazin) reach their minimum at the same point of 11 Å.
source: Strikingly, the two curves reach their minimum at the same point of 11 Å (triangles in Figure 6D) and have identical curvature.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the trapping profile analysis.

claim: Neither M1M nor M8M bis-MTS cross-linker had any effect on activated GluA2-Stg complexes.
source: As predicted, neither bis-MTS cross-linker had any effect on activated GluA2-Stg complexes (M1M: p = 0.1, n = 9; M8M: p = 0.2, n = 9; paired recordings with and without bis-MTS) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an experimental result for active receptors with Stargazin and CTZ.

claim: Docked structures with low Cys666 accessibility segregated into two classes: a loose arrangement and a tighter arrangement of the LBDs.
source: Interestingly, docked structures with low Cys666 accessibility segregated into two classes, a loose arrangement where Cys666 were physically close but sterically hindering each other (with the centre of mass separation of the two active dimers comparable to 5WEO, for example models m17 and m32 in Figure 7D), and a tighter arrangement of the LBDs with V666C close to helix K (with the centre of mass separation of the two active dimers smaller than in 5WEO, for example m223 and m265 in Figure 7D), not unlike the structure of the V666C mutant LBD bound with fluorowillardine (5JEI) (Salazar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from computational docking experiments.

claim: Active GluA2-Stg complexes could avoid cross-linking by adopting more compact LBD arrangements and by preferring conformations which shield V666C SG groups.
source: Thus, docked structures lead us to hypothesize that active GluA2-Stg complexes could avoid cross-linking not just by adopting more compact LBD arrangements, but also by preferring conformations which shield V666C SG groups.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the docking results.

claim: Bis-MTS cross-linkers show specific combination with two free thiol groups and can in principle report distances, giving them the property of nanometre-scale molecular rulers.
source: These cross-linkers show specific combination with two free thiol groups, provided by cysteine residues that we engineered. The selective reactivity of a series of probes can in principle report distances, giving them the property of nanometre-scale molecular rulers.
evidence: This is a known property of bis-MTS reagents and the rationale for their use.

claim: Bis-MTS cross-linkers exert their effect mainly by preventing the engineered residues from separating more than the extended length of the cross-linker.
source: For this reason, we used bis-MTS ranging from 7 to 18 Å in length (M1M – M10M). Our results show an optimum (inhibitory) effect of the cross-linkers at position V666C, with M10M not producing as strong effect as shorter cross-linkers. This is inconsistent with the interpretation of the universal inhibitor and suggests bis-MTS cross-linkers exert their effect mainly by preventing the engineered residues from separating more than the extended length of the cross-linker.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the length-dependent effects of crosslinkers.

claim: All bis-MTS cross-linkers, when applied to the mutants at the inter-dimer LBD interface, inhibited the current.
source: All bis-MTS cross-linkers, when applied to the mutants at the inter-dimer LBD interface, inhibited the current, albeit to a different degree depending on the functional state of the receptors.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: To date all inter-dimer traps have been inhibitory, regardless of the nature of the constraint.
source: However, to date all inter-dimer traps have been inhibitory. Inhibition seems independent of the nature of the constraint, whether disulphide bonds (Plested and Mayer, 2009; Yelshanskaya et al., 2016), metal bridges (Lau et al., 2013; Baranovic et al., 2016), flexible or rigid bis-MTS cross-linkers (this study).
evidence: This is an observation summarizing results from this and previous studies.

claim: The mechanism behind the inhibition by inter-dimer crosslinking remains unclear.
source: The mechanism behind this inhibition remains frustratingly unclear, limiting the interpretation of the cross-linking approach used in this study.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in understanding the results.

claim: The shallow trapping profile of desensitized AMPA receptors indicates a structural ensemble of conformations broadly in agreement with multiple desensitized states.
source: The shallow trapping profile of desensitized AMPA receptors indicates a structural ensemble of conformations broadly in agreement with multiple desensitized states (Meyerson et al., 2014; Robert and Howe, 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trapping profile data in relation to previous studies.

claim: The longest cross-linker (18 Å) was the slowest one to act on desensitized receptors, indicating that more 'open' conformations are not readily available for cross-linking but slowly get populated during prolonged exposures to agonist.
source: However, the longest cross-linker (18 Å) was the slowest one to act on desensitized receptors, indicating that this conformation, and more 'open' ones, are not readily available for cross-linking, but slowly get populated during prolonged exposures to agonist.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetics of crosslinking with M10M.

claim: The strongest cross-linking effect in the active state was achieved by the 12–15 Å-long bis-MTS, suggesting inter-dimer V666C residues are closer together in the active state than 19 Å predicted by the structural model.
source: There, the strongest cross-linking effect was achieved by the 12–15 Å-long bis-MTS (green in Figure 8B). This suggests inter-dimer V666C residues are closer together in the active state than 19 Å, predicted by the structural model (PDB: 4UQ6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the active state trapping profile compared to structural models.

claim: The presence of Stargazin led to universal attenuation of the cross-linking effect for all bis-MTS lengths and both functional states.
source: The presence of Stg lead to universal attenuation of the cross-linking effect, for all bis-MTS lengths and both functional states, desensitized and active (orange and blue in Figure 8A and B, respectively).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results with Stargazin.

claim: The longest crosslinker (M10M) produced the least trapping of GluA2-Stargazin complexes, even following long exposures (~3 min).
source: The longest crosslinker (M10M) produced the least trapping, even following long exposures (~3 min). Thus, the LBD layer could not be modulated by bis-MTS cross-linkers for majority of these receptors.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the effect of M10M on receptors with Stargazin.

claim: In the desensitized state, the shape of the trapping profile is the same with or without Stargazin, with both parabola reaching a minimum point at 11 Å, in excellent agreement with the structure of desensitized GluA2-Stg complex.
source: In the desensitized state, the shape of the trapping profile is the same, with or without Stg (Figure 8A), with both parabola reaching a minimum point at 11 Å (triangles in Figure 8A). This is in excellent agreement with the structure of desensitized GluA2-Stg complex (PDB: 5VOV).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with structural data.

claim: In the active state with Stargazin, the results deviate from the available full-length active structures, with both short and long bis-MTS reagents failing to inhibit currents in the first minute of trapping.
source: In the active state with Stg, our results deviate from the available full-length active structures. Both short and long (7 or 15 Å) bis-MTS reagents failed to inhibit currents in the first minute of trapping, indicating more compact LBD arrangements over this timescale than obtained in the structures.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with structural models.

claim: If structures can be obtained in a time-resolved manner in milliseconds following glutamate exposure, the results suggest they should be more compact than structures solved to date.
source: In other words, if structures can be obtained in a time-resolved manner in milliseconds following glutamate exposure (Unwin, 1995), our results suggest they should be more compact than structures solved to date.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about what time-resolved structures might show.

claim: Active receptors could be trapped by zinc bridges in compact arrangements.
source: First, we previously showed that active receptors could be trapped by zinc bridges in compact arrangements (Baranovic et al., 2016).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Docking data show that conformations which reduce the accessibility of the V666C side chains are accessible to the active LBDs.
source: Docking data in Figure 7D–E show that conformations which reduce the accessibility of the V666C side chains are indeed accessible to the active LBDs.
evidence: This is a result from the computational docking experiments.

claim: These docked arrangements are more compact than the available structures of the full-length receptor in the active state.
source: These arrangements are more compact than the available structures of the full-length receptor in the active state (Chen et al., 2017; Twomey et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is a comparison of docking results with published structures.

claim: The presence of Stargazin increases the current carried by receptors with one or two active subunits.
source: But the presence of Stg (Coombs et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2014) increases the current carried by receptors with one or two active subunits.
evidence: This is a known effect of Stargazin supported by citations.

claim: Single channel recordings of GluA2 with Stargazin reveal that the conductance from two subunits with desensitization blocked should be on average about 40% of a full opening but with Popen < 1.
source: Single channel recordings of GluA2 with Stg reveal that the conductance from two subunits, with desensitization blocked, should be on average about 40% of a full opening but with Popen < 1 (Coombs et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from a cited study.

claim: Physiological activation and desensitization of AMPA receptors takes place on a millisecond timescale.
source: Physiological activation and desensitization of AMPA receptors takes place on a millisecond timescale.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMPA receptor kinetics.

claim: Desensitized states trapped by bis-MTS cross-linkers take tens of minutes to recover.
source: The fast gating contrasts desensitized states trapped by bis-MTS cross-linkers that take tens of minutes to recover.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the recovery experiments.

claim: For crosslinkers longer than 10 Å, crosslinking in desensitized states is irreversible over 10 min.
source: This idea is supported by the cut-off that we observe – for crosslinkers longer than 10 Å, crosslinking in desensitized states is irreversible over 10 min (also in fivefold higher concentration of the reducing agent).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about recovery from crosslinking.

claim: In reducing conditions, AMPA receptors recover from disulphide crosslinking at the same sites in hundreds of milliseconds.
source: In addition, in reducing conditions, AMPA receptors recover from disulphide crosslinking at the same sites in hundreds of milliseconds (Lau et al., 2013; Salazar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from previous studies by the authors.

claim: AMPA receptors at synapses, exposed to brief glutamate transients and in complex with auxiliary subunits, are unlikely to undergo extreme conformational changes.
source: Assuming that the length of the bis-MTS cross-linkers reflects level of structural rearrangements and following the trend plotted in Figure 4H, this suggests that AMPA receptors at synapses, exposed to brief glutamate transients and in complex with auxiliary subunits, are unlikely to undergo extreme conformational changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stability of trapped states and physiological conditions.

claim: Long agonist exposures of minutes to hours are standard in structural biology experiments and could contribute to the prevalence of more 'open' conformations in full-length structures without auxiliary subunits.
source: Long agonist exposures of minutes to hours are standard in structural biology experiments and could, thus, contribute to the prevalence of more 'open' conformations in full-length structures without auxiliary subunits (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a speculation about how structural biology methods might bias observed conformations.

claim: Long exposures to agonists are at odds with synaptic conditions where AMPA receptors see glutamate on a millisecond timescale before it is actively cleared by transporters.
source: However, long exposures to agonists are at odds with synaptic conditions where AMPA receptors see glutamate on a millisecond timescale, before it is actively cleared by transporters (Clements, 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental conditions and physiological conditions, supported by a citation.

claim: Any large structural rearrangements of the extracellular domains would need to be accommodated by the crowded synaptic environment and potential presynaptic interaction partners.
source: Furthermore, any large structural rearrangements of the extracellular domains would need to be accommodated by the crowded synaptic environment (High et al., 2015; Tao et al., 2018) and potential presynaptic interaction partners (Saglietti et al., 2007; Elegheert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a consideration about physical constraints at synapses, supported by citations.

claim: When in complex with auxiliary subunits, no functional state of AMPA receptors necessitates large domain movements, and compact arrangements of the extracellular layer can sustain the gating process.
source: When in complex with auxiliary subunits, no functional state of AMPA receptors necessitates large domain movements, and compact arrangements of the extracellular layer can sustain the gating process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with Stargazin.

claim: Extracellular domains of synaptic AMPA receptors are unlikely to undergo large structural rearrangements during synaptic transmission and instead work in a fairly compact conformational regime, unless faced with long exposures to glutamate in pathological conditions.
source: We conclude that extracellular domains of synaptic AMPA receptors are unlikely to undergo large structural rearrangements during synaptic transmission and instead work in a fairly compact conformational regime, unless faced with long exposures to glutamate in pathological conditions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all the experimental findings.
